expectedText:
PERSONAL LIABILITY OF DIRECTORS, OFFICERS, SHAREHOLDERS, AND LLC MEMBERS FOR TORTS THEY PERSONALLY COMMIT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Widgets, Inc. · Jordan Lee

PERSONAL TORT LIABILITY OF DIRECTORS, OFFICERS, AND OWNERS — APPLICABILITY NOTE
This information sheet concerns Acme Widgets, Inc. and the separate question of when a person who acts for a California corporation or limited liability company can be held personally liable, in tort, to someone outside the entity. It records that Jordan Lee, whose position with Acme Widgets, Inc. is stated here as president, director, and majority shareholder, is the person whose potential personal liability is under consideration, and that the conduct in question, if any has been identified, is described as: supervision of the March 2026 roof installation at 123 Main Street. The sheet sets out what the California Supreme Court and the Courts of Appeal have said about the subject: that director, officer, or shareholder status by itself neither creates vicarious liability for the entity's torts nor immunizes the person from liability for tortious conduct in which the person personally participates; what a plaintiff must show to state a tort claim against a director or officer individually, including the requirement that the act breach a duty owed to the third person and not merely a duty owed to the entity; how this doctrine differs from alter ego or “piercing the corporate veil” liability; the limited role of the statutory business judgment rule in claims brought by outsiders; the agency-law roots of the rule and Civil Code section 2343; and the limited liability company counterpart in Corporations Code section 17703.04, subdivisions (a) and (c). Whether Jordan Lee did or did not participate in, authorize, direct, or knowingly consent to any conduct, whether any conduct was tortious, whether any duty was owed to any particular person, and what a court would decide on any set of facts are questions this sheet does not address and does not determine.

HOLDING OFFICE IS NEITHER A SOURCE OF LIABILITY NOR A SHIELD FROM IT
California law starts from two propositions that point in opposite directions. First, a person does not become liable for a corporation's torts merely because that person is a director or officer of the corporation: the California Supreme Court has said it is well settled that corporate directors cannot be held vicariously liable for the corporation's torts in which they do not participate, and that their liability, if any, stems from their own tortious conduct rather than from their status in the enterprise. The Supreme Court has also quoted the older formulation that directors or officers do not incur personal liability for torts of the corporation merely by reason of their official position, unless they participate in the wrong or authorize or direct that it be done. Second, and by the same logic, holding office is not a shield: the Court has said that director status neither immunizes a person from individual liability nor subjects him or her to vicarious liability, and that while the corporate form was intended to insulate stockholders from personal liability for corporate acts and officers from liability on corporate contracts, the corporate fiction was never intended to insulate officers from liability for their own tortious conduct. A Court of Appeal has restated the same pair of propositions in a single sentence, saying that corporate director or officer status neither immunizes a person from personal liability for tortious conduct nor subjects him or her to vicarious liability for such acts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "It is well settled that corporate directors cannot be held vicariously liable for the corporation’s torts in which they do not participate. Their liability, if any, stems from their own tortious conduct, not from their status as directors or officers of the enterprise."
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 503 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "“[A]n officer or director will not be liable for torts in which he does not personally participate, of which he has no knowledge, or to which he has not consented."
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 503 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "the individual officer or director will be immune unless he authorizes, directs, or in some meaningful sense actively participates in the wrongful conduct.”"
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 504 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "“Directors or officers of a corporation do not incur personal liability for torts of the corporation merely by reason of their official position, unless they participate in the wrong or authorize or direct that it be done.”"
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 507 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "Director status therefore neither immunizes a person from individual liability nor subjects him or her to vicarious liability."
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 505 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "the corporate fiction, however, was never intended to insulate officers from liability for their own tortious conduct."
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 508 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "Corporate director or officer status neither immunizes a person from personal liability for tortious conduct nor subjects him or her to vicarious liability for such acts."
  — PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368, 78 Cal.App.4th at p. 1379 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2274529/pmc-inc-v-kadisha/)
  Known gap: These are appellate statements of California common law, not statutes; they describe when a claim may be maintained against an individual and do not determine whether any particular person participated in anything or whether any conduct was tortious. The Supreme Court's sentence beginning “[A]n officer or director will not be liable for torts in which he does not personally participate” is language the Court quoted from a federal district court decision applying California law (Teledyne Industries, Inc. v. Eon Corp. (S.D.N.Y. 1975) 401 F.Supp. 729), and the sentence beginning “Directors or officers of a corporation do not incur personal liability” is language the Court quoted from its own earlier decision in United States Liab. Ins. Co. v. Haidinger-Hayes, Inc. (1970) 1 Cal.3d 586; neither Teledyne nor Haidinger-Hayes was separately fetched for this sheet, and the words are quoted as they appear in the opinions that reproduce them. The Frances T. quotation ending “will be immune unless he authorizes, directs, or in some meaningful sense actively participates in the wrongful conduct” is the continuation of the Teledyne sentence quoted immediately before it; the reporter's star-pagination marker that falls between the two fragments in the published text has been omitted by splitting the passage into two quotations rather than altering either one.

WHAT COUNTS AS PARTICIPATION: DIRECTING, AUTHORIZING, OR KNOWINGLY CONSENTING
The line California courts draw is participation. The Supreme Court has said that directors are jointly liable with the corporation and may be joined as defendants if they personally directed or participated in the tortious conduct, and that directors are liable to third persons injured by their own tortious conduct regardless of whether they acted on behalf of the corporation and regardless of whether the corporation is also liable. A Court of Appeal has held that participation need not be direct action alone: an officer's or director's participation in tortious conduct may be shown by knowing consent to or approval of unlawful acts, and that court stated that knowing consent to, or approval or authorization of, wrongdoing suffices to impose personal liability. The same court noted that directors and officers may also be held personally liable as conspirators for violating their own duties toward persons injured by the corporation's tort. On the other side of the line, another Court of Appeal contrasted a corporate policy decision carried out by someone else with the case before it, where the company's president had personally participated in and directed the construction work that caused the plaintiffs' property damage; there, the court said, the allegations of direct participation and decisionmaking prevented the officer from using the corporate veil to shield himself from personal liability.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Directors are jointly liable with the corporation and may be joined as defendants if they personally directed or participated in the tortious conduct."
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 504 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "Directors are liable to third persons injured by their own tortious conduct regardless of whether they acted on behalf of the corporation and regardless of whether the corporation is also liable."
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 504 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "A corporate director or officer’s participation in tortious conduct may be shown not solely by direct action but also by knowing consent to or approval of unlawful acts."
  — PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368, 78 Cal.App.4th at p. 1380 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2274529/pmc-inc-v-kadisha/)
  "Further, an officer’s or director’s knowing consent to, or approval or authorization of, wrongdoing suffices to impose personal liability."
  — PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368, 78 Cal.App.4th at p. 1388 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2274529/pmc-inc-v-kadisha/)
  "In addition, corporate directors and officers may be held personally liable, as conspirators, for violating their own duties towards persons injured by the corporation’s tort."
  — PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368, 78 Cal.App.4th at p. 1380 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2274529/pmc-inc-v-kadisha/)
  "Appellants’ allegations here show that respondent did not merely make a corporate policy decision which was carried out by someone else."
  — Michaelis v. Benavides (1998) 61 Cal.App.4th 681, 61 Cal.App.4th at p. 686 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2257967/michaelis-v-benavides/)
  "He personally participated in and directed the construction of appellants’ patio and driveway."
  — Michaelis v. Benavides (1998) 61 Cal.App.4th 681, 61 Cal.App.4th at p. 686 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2257967/michaelis-v-benavides/)
  "In addition, appellants alleged facts indicating respondent may be personally liable for the negligent act by his direct participation and decisionmaking in the construction of the patio and driveway. These allegations, together with the parties’ stipulation, prevent respondent from using the corporate veil to shield himself from personal liability."
  — Michaelis v. Benavides (1998) 61 Cal.App.4th 681, 61 Cal.App.4th at p. 686 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2257967/michaelis-v-benavides/)
  Known gap: These sentences state the standard for pleading and proving participation; they do not measure any particular person's conduct. The Michaelis discussion arose on a nonsuit following a stipulation, for purposes of that motion, that the officer was individually negligent, so the court was describing what the pleadings and the stipulation permitted rather than making findings after trial. The PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha statements arose on review of a summary judgment, where the court held only that triable issues of material fact existed and reversed; it did not decide that the defendants were liable. Two of the quoted PMC sentences summarize holdings the court drew from earlier decisions (including Spahn v. Guild Industries Corp. (1979) 94 Cal.App.3d 143, Doctors’ Co. v. Superior Court (1989) 49 Cal.3d 39, and Wyatt v. Union Mortgage Co. (1979) 24 Cal.3d 773) that were not separately fetched for this sheet.

THIS IS NOT ALTER EGO LIABILITY, AND IT DOES NOT REQUIRE DISREGARDING THE ENTITY
California treats personal liability for one's own tortious conduct as a separate doctrine from alter ego, or “piercing the corporate veil.” The Supreme Court said so expressly: this liability does not depend on the same grounds as piercing the corporate veil — inadequate capitalization, for instance — but rather on the officer's or director's personal participation in or specific authorization of the tortious act. A Court of Appeal has repeated the point in its own words, saying that the legal fiction of the corporation as an independent entity was never intended to insulate officers and directors from liability for their own tortious conduct, and quoting the Supreme Court's statement that the corporate form and the special benefit of limited liability are intended to insulate stockholders from personal liability for corporate acts and officers from liability for corporate contracts. In the Supreme Court's explanation of why the rule exists, without it a director could inflict injuries upon others and then escape liability behind the shield of his or her representative character, even though the corporation might be insolvent or irresponsible.

  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 504 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "The legal fiction of the corporation as an independent entity was never intended to insulate officers and directors from liability for their own tortious conduct."
  — PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368, 78 Cal.App.4th at p. 1380 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2274529/pmc-inc-v-kadisha/)
  "a director could inflict injuries upon others and then escape liability behind the shield of his or her representative character, even though the corporation might be insolvent or irresponsible."
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 505 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)

This corpus's separate alter ego information sheet addresses the unity-of-interest and inequitable-result test and the statutory parity provision for LLC members, which are not repeated here. The quoted phrase “piercing the corporate veil” appears in the Supreme Court's opinion inside the court's own quotation marks, and those marks are reproduced as published. The PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha sentence quoted here cites both Frances T. and Michaelis v. Benavides; the Michaelis “corporate veil” language is quoted separately in the participation clause of this sheet rather than duplicated here.

THE ACT MUST BREACH A DUTY OWED TO THE INJURED PERSON, NOT ONLY A DUTY OWED TO THE COMPANY
Participation alone does not end the inquiry. The Supreme Court has restated the traditional rule that directors are not personally liable to third persons for negligence amounting merely to a breach of a duty the officer owes to the corporation alone; the act must also constitute a breach of duty owed to the third person, and more must be shown than breach of the officer's duty to the corporation. The Court drew the distinction in general terms: a director's fiduciary duty to the corporation and its beneficiaries is one thing, and the director's ordinary duty to take care not to injure third parties is another. In the same discussion the Court noted a second traditional limitation drawn from its earlier decision — that liability imposed on agents for active participation in tortious acts of the principal has been mostly restricted to cases involving physical injury rather than pecuniary harm to third persons. A Court of Appeal applied both limitations in a case where a company president was alleged to have negligently built a patio and driveway, distinguishing the earlier Supreme Court decision on the ground that the features that had absolved the officer there — breach of a duty to the corporation alone, nontortious personal conduct, and the absence of physical damage — were not present.

  "In other words, a distinction must be made between the director’s fiduciary duty to the corporation (and its beneficiaries) and the director’s ordinary duty to take care not to injure third parties."
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 506 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "“Liability imposed upon agents for active participation in tortious acts of the principal have been mostly restricted to cases involving physical injury, not pecuniary harm, to third persons [citations].”"
  — Frances T. v. Village Green Owners Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 490, 42 Cal.3d at p. 505 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1318232/frances-t-v-village-green-owners-assn/)
  "which absolved the defendant corporate officer of personal liability — the breach of duty to the corporation alone, the nontortious personal conduct, and the absence of physical damage — do not exist here."
  — Michaelis v. Benavides (1998) 61 Cal.App.4th 681, 61 Cal.App.4th at p. 687 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2257967/michaelis-v-benavides/)
  "The instant circumstances involve a corporate officer’s personal tortious conduct, which conduct breached a duty of care to a third party and caused the third party to suffer physical damage to his property."
  — Michaelis v. Benavides (1998) 61 Cal.App.4th 681, 61 Cal.App.4th at p. 687 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2257967/michaelis-v-benavides/)

The bracketed capital letter in the quotation “[T]he act must also constitute a breach of duty owed to the third person” is the Supreme Court's own alteration of the language it was quoting from United States Liab. Ins. Co. v. Haidinger-Hayes, Inc. (1970) 1 Cal.3d 586, and the bracketed word “[citations]” in the physical-injury quotation is the Court's own substitution for the authorities it cited; Haidinger-Hayes itself was not separately fetched for this sheet. The quotation about physical rather than pecuniary harm describes where courts had mostly imposed such liability, not a categorical bar, and the Supreme Court in the same passage analyzed the pecuniary-loss claim before it under agency principles. One Michaelis quotation is split around the italicized case name “Haidinger-Hayes” as published; the words quoted here are the sentence's remainder, which reads continuously in the opinion.

WHAT THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT REQUIRES A PLAINTIFF TO SHOW AGAINST A DIRECTOR INDIVIDUALLY
The California Supreme Court stated the showing required to maintain a tort claim against a director in his or her personal capacity. A plaintiff must first show either that the director specifically authorized, directed, or participated in the allegedly tortious conduct, or that although the directors specifically knew or reasonably should have known that some hazardous condition or activity under their control could injure the plaintiff, they negligently failed to take or order appropriate action to avoid the harm. The Court added a second, cumulative requirement: the plaintiff must also allege and prove that an ordinarily prudent person, knowing what the director knew at that time, would not have acted similarly under the circumstances. The Court coupled that standard with a defense of reasonable reliance, stating that even if their conduct leads directly to the tortious injury of a third party, directors are not personally liable in tort unless their action, including any claimed reliance on expert advice, was clearly unreasonable under the circumstances known to them at the time. Separately, the Court described the duty side of the same analysis, saying that like any other employee, directors individually owe a duty of care, independent of the corporate entity's own duty, to refrain from acting in a manner that creates an unreasonable risk of personal injury to third parties.

The standard as quoted is addressed to directors; the opinion and later Court of Appeal decisions apply parallel reasoning to officers, but the words quoted here say “director.” Two of the quotations are consecutive fragments of a single sentence separated in the published text by an internal citation, quoted separately so that no omitted citation is silently absorbed into a quotation. Whether any person had the knowledge, control, or opportunity to act that the standard describes is not addressed here.

THE STATUTORY BUSINESS JUDGMENT RULE GOVERNS DUTIES TO THE ENTITY, NOT THE DUTY OWED TO INJURED OUTSIDERS
Directors sued personally by an outsider have argued that the statutory standard of care for directors — the business judgment rule — measures what they owe to the injured person. The California Supreme Court rejected that argument. It said it must reject the assertion that a director's liability to third persons is controlled by the statutory duty of care the director owes to the corporation, the standard defined in Corporations Code section 7231 (the nonprofit mutual benefit corporation counterpart of section 309 for business corporations). That statutory standard of care, commonly referred to as the business judgment rule, applies to parties — particularly shareholders and creditors — to whom the directors owe a fiduciary obligation, and the Court held that it does not abrogate the common law duty which every person owes to others, that is, a duty to refrain from conduct that imposes an unreasonable risk of injury on third parties. As restated by a Court of Appeal quoting the same opinion, corporate officers have a societal duty, like any other citizen, to refrain from acts that are unreasonably risky to third persons even when their shareholders or creditors would agree that such conduct serves the institution's best interests.

  Known gap: The Supreme Court decided this point in a case involving a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation, so the statute it named is Corporations Code section 7231; the Court elsewhere in the same opinion referred to sections 7231 and 309 together, and this corpus's separate business-judgment-rule information sheet addresses section 309 for business corporations. The holding quoted here concerns what standard governs a third party's tort claim; it does not address the business judgment rule's operation in claims by the entity or its owners, and it does not determine whether any conduct was unreasonably risky. The final quotation is the Court of Appeal's reproduction of a passage from footnote 12 of the Supreme Court's opinion; the footnote text is quoted as it appears in the later opinion, which was independently fetched, rather than from the footnote as separately paginated.

THE RULE'S ROOTS IN AGENCY LAW AND CIVIL CODE SECTION 2343
California courts locate this rule in the law of agency rather than in corporate law alone. The Supreme Court said the rule has its roots in the law of agency, that directors are said to be agents of their corporate principal, and quoted the proposition that the agent is liable for the agent's own acts regardless of whether the principal is liable or amenable to judicial action. A Court of Appeal restated the same lineage, saying that the Supreme Court has held that the rule imposing liability on an officer or director for participation in or authorization of tortious conduct has its roots in agency law, that an agent is liable for her or his own acts regardless whether the principal is also liable, and quoting the governing statute: Civil Code section 2343 provides that one who assumes to act as an agent is responsible to third persons as a principal for acts in the course of the agency in enumerated cases and in no others, the third of which is when the agent's acts are wrongful in their nature. That court added that this rule applies to officers and directors. Because the rule is an agency rule, it is not limited by title: the same Court of Appeal said that a corporate officer or director, like any other person, owes a duty to refrain from injuring others.

  Known gap: Civil Code section 2343 is quoted here from the California Legislative Information text of the section and, within the Court of Appeal's opinion, as that court reproduced it with its own bracketed paragraph markers and ellipsis for the omitted subdivisions 1 and 2. The statute is an agency statute of general application, enacted in 1872; it is quoted as evidence of the rule's statutory anchor, not as a corporations statute, and it does not by itself establish that any person acted as an agent or that any act was wrongful in its nature. The Supreme Court's quoted sentence about an agent's liability is language it quoted from James v. Marinship Corp. (1944) 25 Cal.2d 721, which was not separately fetched for this sheet.

THE LLC STATUTE SAYS THE SAME THING: A MEMBER'S OWN TORTIOUS CONDUCT IS NOT COVERED BY THE SHIELD
For limited liability companies the point is written into the statute. Corporations Code section 17703.04 provides that the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise, are solely those of the company to which they relate, and do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or the manager acting as a manager. Subdivision (c) then states the limit of that shield: nothing in the section is to be construed to affect the liability of a member of a limited liability company to third parties for the member's participation in tortious conduct, or liability under the terms of a written guarantee or other contractual obligation entered into by the member other than an operating agreement. The statutory structure therefore tracks the corporate case law — status as a member or manager is not itself a source of liability for the company's obligations, and the shield the section provides is not addressed to a member's own participation in tortious conduct.

California law starts from two propositions that point in opposite directions. First, a person does not become liable for a corporation's torts merely because that person is a director or officer of the corporation: the California Supreme Court has said it is well settled that corporate directors cannot be held vicariously liable for the corporation's torts in which they do not participate, and that their liability, if any, stems from their own tortious conduct rather than from their status in the enterprise. The Supreme Court has also quoted the older formulation that directors or officers do not incur personal liability for torts of the corporation merely by reason of their official position, unless they participate in the wrong or authorize or direct that it be done. Second, and by the same logic, holding office is not a shield: the Court has said that director status neither immunizes a person from individual liability nor subjects him or her to vicarious liability, and that while the corporate form was intended to insulate stockholders from personal liability for corporate acts and officers from liability on corporate contracts, the corporate fiction was never intended to insulate officers from liability for their own tortious conduct. A Court of Appeal has restated the same pair of propositions in a single sentence, saying that corporate director or officer status neither immunizes a person from personal liability for tortious conduct nor subjects him or her to vicarious liability for such acts.

Separately, the Court described the duty side of the same analysis, saying that like any other employee, directors individually owe a duty of care, independent of the corporate entity's own duty, to refrain from acting in a manner that creates an unreasonable risk of personal injury to third parties.

It said it must reject the assertion that a director's liability to third persons is controlled by the statutory duty of care the director owes to the corporation, the standard defined in Corporations Code section 7231 (the nonprofit mutual benefit corporation counterpart of section 309 for business corporations). expectedJSON.gap: Civil Code section 2343 is quoted here from the California Legislative Information text of the section and, within the Court of Appeal's opinion, as that court reproduced it with its own bracketed paragraph markers and ellipsis for the omitted subdivisions 1 and 2. The statute is an agency statute of general application, enacted in 1872; it is quoted as evidence of the rule's statutory anchor, not as a corporations statute, and it does not by itself establish that any person acted as an agent or that any act was wrongful in its nature. The Supreme Court's quoted sentence about an agent's liability is language it quoted from James v. Marinship Corp. (1944) 25 Cal.2d 721, which was not separately fetched for this sheet.

expectedJSON.body: For limited liability companies the point is written into the statute. Corporations Code section 17703.04 provides that the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise, are solely those of the company to which they relate, and do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or the manager acting as a manager. Subdivision (c) then states the limit of that shield: nothing in the section is to be construed to affect the liability of a member of a limited liability company to third parties for the member's participation in tortious conduct, or liability under the terms of a written guarantee or other contractual obligation entered into by the member other than an operating agreement. The statutory structure therefore tracks the corporate case law — status as a member or manager is not itself a source of liability for the company's obligations, and the shield the section provides is not addressed to a member's own participation in tortious conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Corporations Code § 17703.04(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: All of the following apply to debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise:

citations.case: Cal. Corporations Code § 17703.04(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: They are solely the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the limited liability company to which the debts, obligations, or other liabilities relate.

citations.case: Cal. Corporations Code § 17703.04(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: They do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or manager acting as a manager for the limited liability company.

citations.case: Cal. Corporations Code § 17703.04(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall be construed to affect the liability of a member of a limited liability company to third parties for the member’s participation in tortious conduct, or pursuant to the terms of a written guarantee or other contractual obligation entered into by the member, other than an operating agreement.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes the statute's text only. Subdivision (c) speaks of a “member”; the subdivision (a) shield speaks of both members and managers, and the statute does not contain a parallel tortious-conduct sentence naming managers. Subdivision (b) of the same section, which subjects LLC members to common-law alter ego liability on the same terms as corporate shareholders and carves out the failure to hold meetings, is addressed in this corpus's separate alter ego information sheet and is not quoted here. The statute states what it does not affect; it does not itself define participation in tortious conduct, and whether any member participated in anything is not addressed by this sheet. The section's application to foreign limited liability companies and to the insurance and undertaking requirement in subdivision (d) is outside this clause.

expectedJSON.body: The same framework has been applied to people whose connection to the company is ownership or investment rather than day-to-day management. A Court of Appeal framed the question presented as whether, as shareholders, officers, and directors of a corporation, the defendants could be held personally liable for misappropriation of trade secrets, unfair competition, or interference with prospective economic advantage. The court stated that shareholders are likewise not normally liable for a corporation's torts, but that personal liability may attach to them when they specifically direct or authorize the wrongful acts. On the facts before it, the court held that a corporate officer or director may be liable for an intentional tort where the officer or director purchased or invested in a corporation whose principal assets were the result of unlawful conduct, took control of the corporation and appointed personnel to run it while it was engaging in unlawful conduct, and did so with knowledge or, as to trade secret misappropriation, reason to know of the unlawful conduct. The court also observed the damages consequence of participation in an intentional tort: all persons shown to have participated in an intentional tort are liable for the full amount of the damages suffered.

citations.case: PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368
citations.quote: The question presented is whether, as shareholders, officers and directors of a corporation, defendants can be held personally liable for misappropriation of trade secrets, unfair competition, or interference with prospective economic advantage.

citations.case: PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368
citations.quote: We hold that a corporate officer or director may be liable for an intentional tort if: (1) the officer or director purchased or invested in the corporation the principal assets of which were the result of unlawful conduct; (2) the officer or director took control of the corporation and appointed personnel to run the corporation, which was engaging in unlawful conduct; and (3) the officer or director did so with knowledge or, with respect to trade secret misappropriation, when she or he had reason to know, of the unlawful conduct.

citations.case: PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368
citations.quote: Shareholders are likewise not normally liable for a corporation’s torts, “but personal liability may attach to them . . . when [they] specifically direct[] or authorize the wrongful acts.”

citations.case: PMC, Inc. v. Kadisha (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 1368
citations.quote: All persons who are shown to have participated in an intentional tort are liable for the full amount of the damages suffered.

expectedJSON.gap: This holding comes from a Court of Appeal decision reversing a summary judgment; the court held that triable issues of material fact existed as to the defendants' active meaningful participation in, consent to, or approval of the tortious conduct, and did not decide that the defendants were liable. The three-element formulation quoted here is tied to the facts before that court — investors who bought into a corporation whose principal assets were allegedly misappropriated trade secrets — and is not a general test for investor liability. The sentence about shareholders quotes, inside the court's own sentence, language that court took from Wyatt v. Union Mortgage Co. (1979) 24 Cal.3d 773, including that opinion's bracketed alterations; Wyatt was not separately fetched for this sheet. The full-damages sentence states a joint-liability principle for intentional torts and cites Golden v. Anderson (1967) 256 Cal.App.2d 714, which was likewise not separately fetched.
